text.title: Audit Verdict Set — Output Contract
text.summary: The artefact this methodology produces: a per-wave verdict set in which every adverse verdict carries evidence, every disagreement is recorded as ambiguous, and nothing has been applied — machine-checkable by the bundled validator.

section.title: JSON Schema
section.reference: The same schema as a standalone file, for passing to a structured-output call.
Stdlib validator; enforces the forbidden patterns below and reports field drift.

section.title: Adverse verdicts
section.p: `INCORRECT`, `OUT_OF_SCOPE` and `WEAK` are adverse: they assert a defect in the corpus. `CONFIRMED`, `AMBIGUOUS` and `UNVERIFIABLE` are not. The evidence floor applies to adverse verdicts only, which is what keeps it cheap.

list.item: f1 — an adverse verdict with `evidence` empty, `"none"` or whitespace. The aggregator downgrades it to `AMBIGUOUS`; a file that still contains one means the floor was never applied.
f2 — `applied: true`, or any item carrying an `applied_at` field. This artefact is a proposal set; applying is a separate gated pass.
f3 — a `suspect: true` item with no `verified: true` and no `refuted_by` count. Every suspect must have been through the refute pass or be explicitly recorded as skipped.
f4 — `count` not equal to `len(items)`, or the `by_verdict` totals not summing to `count`. Every number is machine-computed or it is not trusted.
f5 — a `PARSE_ERROR` verdict left in a final file. It means the field-drift normaliser found nothing usable; fix the read or re-run the slice, do not ship it as a tally line.
f6 — duplicate `id` values. Later passes override earlier ones by id, so a duplicate means the merge lost a result.
f7 — a `calibration` block with `sampled` below 5, or with `agreed / sampled` under 0.8, while the wave is presented as final.

example.code: { "wave": 1, "corpus_total": 1460, "count": 3, "applied": false, "field_drift_fallbacks": 0, "by_verdict": {"CONFIRMED": 1, "INCORRECT": 1, "UNVERIFIABLE": 1}, "calibration": {"sampled": 10, "agreed": 9}, "items": [ {"id": "it-0031", "verdict": "CONFIRMED", "suspect": false, "evidence": "src/ch09.md:'…'"}, {"id": "it-0114", "verdict": "INCORRECT", "suspect": true, "verified": true, "refuted_by": 1, "confidence": 0.82, "issue": "keyed option contradicts the cited paragraph", "fix": "change key to B", "evidence": "src/ch09.md:'the second stage precedes …'", "refuter_notes": ["stands: key is wrong", "stands: key is wrong", "unclear"]}, {"id": "it-0207", "verdict": "UNVERIFIABLE", "suspect": true, "verified": true, "refuted_by": 0, "issue": "no source cited and none found", "fix": null, "evidence": "none"} ] }
example.note: `UNVERIFIABLE` is allowed `evidence: "none"` — it is not an adverse verdict, and the absence of a source is the finding.

Six violations: f1 (adverse with no evidence), f2 (`applied: true`), f3 (suspect never refuted), f4 (`count` 4 against 3 items and a by_verdict summing to 3), f5 (`PARSE_ERROR` shipped), f6 (duplicate id). Each of these has been produced by a real run; none of them raises an error anywhere else in the pipeline.

list.item: Every adverse verdict quotes a source or names one.
`applied` is false and no item records an application.
Every suspect carries a refute result.
No `PARSE_ERROR` and no duplicate ids survive the merge.
Calibration recorded before the wave is called final.
